Riesling is a good opening wine, and can contrast hearty dishes through lighter weight; ideal for summer outdoors.
Even with a fruit soup, adjust the dish so it is not sweeter than the wine.
Gewürztraminer and Riesling succeed with smoked, spicy, salty and slightly sweet dishes where other wines fall flat.
Gewürztraminer is low in acid; avoid very acidic dishes, which make it taste lifeless.
Gewürztraminer overwhelms delicately flavoured seafood or poultry; serve it well chilled.
Viognier is full, high-alcohol and low-acid; pair with aromatic, full-flavoured, somewhat rich foods.
Smoky dishes and dishes featuring peach or apricot support Viognier beautifully.
Chardonnay is perhaps the hardest wine to pair: high alcohol and heavy oak; unoaked or lightly oaked versions are far easier.
Heavily oaked, buttery Chardonnay works best as an aperitif or with simply prepared seafood and lighter meats.
Match Chardonnay mainly on texture: dishes of similar weight and creaminess succeed more reliably than flavour matches.
Avoid chile-spicy dishes with Chardonnay; heat accentuates its alcohol and oak.
Toasted nuts sprinkled on a dish draw it toward an oaky Chardonnay; butter and cream also love it.
Corn and tarragon are secret-weapon ingredients for Chardonnay.
Crisp, higher-acid Chardonnay such as Chablis suits silky oysters, especially with a little cream.
Side ingredients can redirect a pairing: creamy beans and smoky pancetta steer tuna from Pinot Noir to oaked Chardonnay.
White wine can match meat: braised pork with apples and cream suits round, barrel-aged Chardonnay.
Dijon mustard used sparingly is a versatile bridge to many wines, Chardonnay included.
Lighter, fruit-forward Pinot Noir is especially food-friendly; fruity styles even handle seasoned, smoked and mildly spicy dishes.
Pinot Noir is the most flexible red: meat, poultry, vegetarian dishes and some fish such as salmon and ahi.
Lightly aromatic spices harmonise with fruity Pinot Noir; don't overwhelm it with powerful, assertive dishes.
Oily, meaty fish like salmon and tuna have enough fat to coat the tongue and balance a red wine's tannin.
Coffee and vanilla in a sauce heighten almost any red wine, especially ones with some bottle age.
Walnuts soften tannins in young reds and add crunch.
Sangiovese's cherry fruit, acidity and grip suit tomato pastas, grilled meats, sausage, poultry, game and garlicky rustic Italian food.
Sangiovese connects best with simple rustic grilled or roasted dishes; avoid rich intense sauces except with Super Tuscans and Brunello.
Fresh herbs bring out Sangiovese's country character; tomatoes are an excellent bridge.
Sun-dried cherries are a near-universal bridge to reds (Sangiovese, Cabernet, Pinot Noir, Zinfandel, Merlot), amplifying their cherry fruit.
Zinfandel's berry fruit and lively acidity suit grilled meats and spicier food, especially Latin-style dishes.
Very high-alcohol Zinfandel is less food-friendly; too much chile heat clashes with its alcohol.
Zinfandel handles salty dishes better than most reds because its sweet berry fruit contrasts salt.
Match Zinfandel with weightier braised, grilled or smoked dishes and with berry-based fruit sauces.
Syrah: full, round, low-acid, polished tannins; its smoky, peppery, gamey fruit suits meat, game and hearty fare.
Petite Sirah is a different grape from Syrah but pairs with food much the same way.
Syrah shines with robust braises and all kinds of grilled meats; Rhône blends are softer and handle spicier dishes.
Dry rosé is a chilled warm-weather wine for alfresco meals, cold summer dishes and spicy food.
Syrah is the most peppery red, so it marries peppery, intense sauces especially well.
Merlot is often more food-friendly than Cabernet: smooth, round, bright fruit that fits a wide range of foods.
Heavily oaked, tannic Merlot is harder to pair young; Bordeaux blends follow the food affinities of their main grape.
Merlot suits medium-weight dishes more than very heavy food; cooking with Merlot in sauces helps mirror the wine.
A sprinkle of walnuts or pecans reduces the impression of tannin in tannic Merlot.
Colour can help: a deep red dish creates a subconscious link to a red wine.
Keep a fruit sauce less sweet than the wine or the wine seems dry and lifeless; adjust port and sugar to taste.
Soft, supple Merlot suits braises that combine many complementary flavours.
Young Cabernet's power and tannin are hard on food; age brings elegance and better compatibility.
Cabernet generally does poorly with seafood, spicy food and vinegar, except careful use of balsamic.
Match Cabernet to high-quality meat, game or cheese in dishes with focused flavours so the wine is the star.
Fatty meats coat the palate and shield it from young Cabernet's tannin.
Older, mellower Cabernet suits less intense dishes; heavy reduction sauces suit young Cabernet better.
Dishes with a single clear flavour focus show Cabernet best; walnuts and pecans tame young tannins.
Creamy, rich blue cheese like Gorgonzola helps tame a young, tannic Cabernet.
Slight bitterness, as in eggplant, can offset red wine tannin.
Match intensity: an intense balsamic-mushroom sauce parallels a concentrated Cabernet or Syrah.
Earthy porcini mushrooms mellow Cabernet's tannin; juicy lamb supplies flavour and fat.
Taste the sauce with the wine you'll serve; add a touch of balsamic if the sauce is sweeter than the wine.
Dijon mustard and rosemary are especially flattering to Cabernet.
Dessert wines come from very ripe, often botrytised grapes; a 3-4 ounce pour is plenty, and half bottles suit small groups.
Late-harvest Riesling, low in alcohol, is easier to drink after a meal than port and suits delicate desserts.
Don't make the dessert much sweeter than the wine, or the wine tastes dry.
Build menus on contrast and balance: alternate rich courses with lighter or piquant ones rather than stacking richness.
